entries.meaning: A nineteenth-century rural minced oath for confound it or damn it, now almost entirely a costume word. Americans hear it from prospectors, farmers, and cartoon codgers, and use it themselves only for comic effect.
examples: "Consarn it, boy, shut the gate before the whole herd gets out!"
Consarn it, I've lost my reading glasses again.
He kicked the tire and muttered a consarn it under his breath.
"Consarnit, Martha, we talked about this," Grandpa said, mostly to the radio.
Every time the printer jams my dad yells consarn it like he's in a western.
entries.русский: чёрт бы побрал — устар. деревенская замена damn it, сейчас только в шутку
entries.variants: consarnit, consarn, consarned

entries.meaning: A Southern softening of goddamn, used both as an exclamation and as an adjective planted in front of the offending noun. It is mild enough for a church parking lot, which is exactly why it survives.
examples: Dadgum it, I left the cooler sitting on the kitchen counter.
That dadgum dog dug up my tomatoes again.
"Dadgum," he said, looking at the price of gas.
She hit her thumb with the hammer and hollered dadgummit loud enough for the neighbors.
I can't get this dadgum thing to start in the cold.
entries.русский: чёртов, проклятый — диал. (юж.) смягчённое goddamn: и возглас, и определение
entries.variants: dadgummit, dadgum it, dad-gum it, dadblame, dadblasted

entries.meaning: Another scrambling of goddamn it, this one so thoroughly attached to cartoon old-timers that it is now used almost exclusively as a joke. It expresses frustration at something small that has gone wrong.
examples: "Dagnabbit!" he shouted as the ladder slipped sideways.
Dagnabbit, these kids and their music.
I dropped my phone in the sink — dagnabbit.
She shook her fist at the sky like Yosemite Sam. "Dagnabbit, rain again!"
Dagnab it, that's the third time I've had to reset the router.
entries.русский: тьфу ты, чёрт! — устар. смягчённое goddamn it, речь мультяшных стариков
entries.variants: dagnab it, dad-nab it, dagnabbed, dagnabbit all

entries.meaning: A gentle old stand-in for goddamn, alive both as a standalone gripe (doggone it) and as an all-purpose adjective (that doggone cat). It runs warmer and more rueful than angry, and it is the swear of choice for people who do not swear.
examples: Doggone it, the game's been rained out.
That doggone screen door slams every single time.
"Well, doggone," she said when the pie came out perfect.
I doggone near drove past the exit.
He was a doggone good coach, whatever else you say about him.
entries.русский: чёрт возьми; чёртов — разг. мягкая замена goddamn, скорее с досадой, чем со злостью
entries.variants: doggone it, doggonit, doggoned, dad-gone

entries.meaning: A Southern exclamation of astonishment with a churchy ring to it, said over something startling, oversized, or outrageous. It belongs to grandmothers and preachers more than to anyone under fifty.
examples: "Great day in the morning, how much did they charge you for that?"
Great day in the morning — look at the size of that watermelon.
She opened the closet, saw the mess, and said, "Great day in the mornin'."
Great day, I haven't seen you since you were knee-high.
"Great day in the morning!" Aunt Ruby said when the twins walked in.
entries.русский: батюшки светы! — устар. юж. возглас изумления с церковным оттенком
entries.variants: great day, great day in the mornin'
entries.see also: my stars, land sakes, mercy me

entries.meaning: A friendly Western and Southern hello, worn down from how do you do. Outside Texas and the rural West most Americans use it playfully, and it comes with an imaginary hat brim to tip.
examples: "Howdy, neighbor. Can I give you a hand with that?"
Howdy! Long time no see.
He walked into the office in boots and said howdy to everyone.
"Howdy y'all," the driver called through the window.
She answered the phone with a cheerful howdy that gave her away as a Texan.
entries.русский: здорово!, привет! — диал. (юж./зап.) ковбойское «здрасьте», стёртое how do you do
entries.variants: howdy do, howdy-doody, howdy y'all, how do

entries.meaning: A genteel Southern expression of mild astonishment, roughly well, would you look at that. It is used today almost entirely with an arched eyebrow, often by someone doing an impression of a nineteenth-century belle.
examples: "Well I declare, you've grown a foot since Christmas."
I do declare, that is the ugliest lamp I have ever seen.
She fanned herself and said, "I declare, it is hot out."
Well, I do declare — he actually did the dishes.
"I do declare," my grandmother said, reading the letter twice.
entries.русский: ну надо же!, скажите на милость — устар. юж. жеманное удивление
entries.variants: well I declare, I declare, do declare, well, I do declare
entries.see also: my stars, I swanee, well, shut my mouth

entries.meaning: A rural minced oath standing in for I swear, common in the South and in older New England speech. Speakers who thought swearing sinful used it to register surprise or exasperation without actually taking an oath.
examples: "I swanee, that child never stops talking."
I swan, I don't know where the time went.
He looked at the bill and said, "I swanee, they've doubled it."
Well I swan — you're the spitting image of your mother.
"I swanee to goodness, if it isn't one thing it's another."
entries.русский: вот те на!, ей-же-ей — устар. деревенская замена I swear, чтобы не клясться
entries.variants: I swan, I swannee, well I swan, I swanny
entries.see also: I do declare, my stars, land sakes

entries.meaning: An old exclamation of surprise borrowed from the Book of Exodus, where Goshen is the good land given to the Israelites. It survives mainly in the rural South and Midwest and in the speech of church-raised grandparents.
examples: "Land o' Goshen, what happened to your knees?"
Land o' Goshen, I've never seen so much snow in October.
She came around the corner, saw the puppy on the couch, and said, "Land of Goshen."
Land o' Goshen, child, put on a coat.
"Lands o' Goshen, they want four dollars for a doughnut."
entries.русский: Господи помилуй! — устар. возглас удивления, от библейской земли Гесем
entries.variants: land of Goshen, lands o' Goshen
entries.see also: land sakes, heavens to Betsy, mercy me

entries.meaning: A worn-down version of for the Lord's sake that dodges the Lord entirely. It marks surprise, mild alarm, or fond exasperation, and today it reads as unmistakably old-fashioned and rural.
examples: "Land sakes, you scared me half to death!"
My lands, look how tall he's gotten.
She counted the receipts twice. "Land sakes alive, that can't be right."
Sakes alive, it's cold in this house.
"Good land, honey, there's mud all the way up the stairs."
entries.русский: батюшки мои! — устар. сельский возглас удивления, стёртое for the Lord's sake
entries.variants: land sakes alive, sakes alive, my land, my lands, good land, land's sakes
entries.see also: land o' Goshen, mercy me, my stars

entries.meaning: A drawled, softened Lord used for weariness, wonder, or half-scandalized amusement. Doubling it (lordy lordy) adds a shake of the head, and lordy be adds a Southern flourish.
examples: "Lordy, it's been a long week."
Lordy lordy, look who's forty.
She saw the credit card statement and said, "Lawdy."
Lordy be, that boy can eat.
"Lordy, don't get him started on the highway project."
entries.русский: Господи!, ой божечки — разг. протяжное смягчённое Lord: усталость или изумление
entries.variants: lawdy, lordy lordy, lordy be, lawd, lord have mercy
entries.see also: mercy me, good gravy, great day in the morning

entries.meaning: A soft, churchy exclamation of surprise or sympathy, most at home in the mouth of an older Southern woman. It can react to bad news, to a mess, or simply to something too much to take in.
examples: "Mercy me, that's a lot of stairs."
Mercy sakes, honey, you're soaked through.
She read the obituary and murmured, "Mercy."
Have mercy — did you make all of this yourself?
"Mercy me, I forgot the pie in the oven."
entries.русский: Боже мой!, батюшки — устар. мягкий возглас удивления или сочувствия
entries.variants: mercy, mercy sakes, mercy sakes alive, have mercy, land of mercy
entries.see also: lordy, land sakes, heavens to Betsy

entries.meaning: A quaint exclamation of astonishment, the polite cousin of my God. It sounds Victorian, and it is used today mostly by the elderly or by anyone deliberately sounding elderly.
examples: "My stars, you've redone the whole kitchen!"
My stars and garters, I have never heard such nonsense.
She put her hand to her chest. "Oh my stars."
My stars, it's nearly midnight already.
"My stars, if it isn't the prodigal son," Aunt Fern said from the porch.
entries.русский: батюшки светы!, вот те на — устар. жеманное изумление вместо my God
entries.variants: my stars and garters, stars above, oh my stars
entries.see also: heavens to Betsy, I do declare, land sakes

entries.meaning: Originally the worthless husks of corn, now a country-flavored word for two feelings: bashful modesty when you are praised, and mild disappointment when something falls through. Aw shucks is so tied to the first sense that it doubles as an adjective for anyone who plays humble.
examples: "Shucks, it was nothing. Anybody would have done it."
Aw shucks, you didn't have to get me anything.
Shucks, I was hoping they'd still have tickets.
He gave the crowd an aw-shucks grin and stepped up to the mic.
"Shucks now, don't go making a fuss over me."
entries.русский: да ну что вы, ерунда; эх, жаль — разг. смущение от похвалы; лёгкое разочарование
entries.variants: aw shucks, ah shucks, shucks now

entries.meaning: A blend of eternal and damnation that lets a speaker demand an explanation without swearing. It nearly always sits inside a question — what in tarnation, where in tarnation — filling the slot a stronger word would take.
examples: "What in tarnation is going on out here?"
Tarnation! That was my last clean shirt.
Where in tarnation did I put those keys?
"Who in tarnation parked across two spaces?"
He stared at the assembly instructions. "How in tarnation does this go together?"
entries.русский: чёрт, чёрт побери — устар. только в вопросах: what in tarnation = какого чёрта
entries.variants: what in tarnation, in tarnation, who in tarnation, consarned tarnation
entries.see also: consarn it, what in Sam Hill, dagnabbit

entries.meaning: A Southern expression of amazement meaning roughly I stand corrected or I never would have believed it. It is theatrical by nature and is nearly always said with a smile.
examples: "Well, shut my mouth, you were right all along."
He won the whole thing? Shut my mouth.
Well, shut my mouth — she drove all the way from Atlanta just for supper.
"Shut my mouth, if that isn't the fanciest truck in the county."
Well, shut my mouth wide open, they finally paved the road.
entries.русский: ну и ну!, вот это да — устар. юж. «никогда бы не поверил»
entries.variants: shut my mouth, well shut my mouth wide open
entries.see also: I do declare, my stars, great day in the morning

entries.meaning: A long, whistling country exclamation for anything extreme — heat, spice, price, or distance. It sounds admiring and a little overwhelmed at the same time.
examples: "Whoo-wee, that chili will take the roof off your mouth."
Hoo-wee, it must be a hundred degrees out here.
He looked at the estimate and said, "Whoo-wee, that's steep."
Whoo-wee! Did you see how far he hit that ball?
"Woo-wee, boys, we are a long way from home."
entries.русский: ух ты!, ну и ну! — разг. протяжный возглас о чём-то чрезмерном
entries.variants: hoo-wee, woo-wee, whoo-eee

entries.meaning: A Southern plural you that doubles as a call to a room — set in front of an announcement (y'all, listen up) or tacked onto a greeting or goodbye (hey y'all, bye y'all) purely to signal warmth and shared ground. Its spelling starts arguments: the apostrophe replaces the missing ou of you, so y'all is right and ya'll is not.
examples: "Y'all, listen up — the bus leaves in ten minutes."
Hey y'all, come on in, food's on the table.
Y'all! You are not going to believe who I just saw.
Thanks for coming out, y'all. Drive safe.
All y'all need to be in the van by six.
entries.русский: вы (мн. ч.) — диал. (юж.) южное you во множественном числе; и обращение к компании
entries.variants: all y'all, y'all listen up, hey y'all, yall

entries.meaning: An emphatic country yes, built from yes, sir and then decorated. Yessiree bob is the fullest form, and the Bob is nobody in particular. It confirms something with cheerful finality, often about a fact the speaker is proud of.
examples: "Did you catch anything?" "Yessiree, four of them."
Yessiree bob, that's my grandson on the poster.
He nodded slowly. "Yes siree, she built that porch herself."
Yessiree, thirty-two years at the same plant.
"Is this the last one?" "Yessiree bob, we're done."
entries.русский: так точно!, а как же! — устар. эмфатическое деревенское «да»
entries.variants: yes siree, yessiree bob, yes sirree Bob, yessir

entries.meaning: A rural New England and Midwestern oath from the 1800s, built on the same pattern as by golly and by gum. It emphasizes a statement the speaker is sure of, and today it survives mostly in period fiction and in deliberate hayseed imitations.
examples: "By cracky, that's the biggest pumpkin I've ever seen."
We'll get this barn up by Sunday, by cracky, if I have to nail it myself.
By cracky, the old truck started on the first try.
"You're right, by cracky," the old man said, slapping the counter.
He tasted the cider and declared, "By cracky, that's the good stuff."
entries.русский: ей-богу!, чёрт возьми — устар. деревенская божба для нажима на сказанное
entries.variants: by crackey, by cracky now
entries.see also: by golly, by gum, by jingo

entries.meaning: Golly is a nineteenth-century dodge around saying God, and by golly is the emphatic frame built from it. Alone, golly registers innocent surprise; with by, it insists that something is true or that you really will do it.
examples: "By golly, you did it!"
Golly, that's a lot of stairs for one building.
If they won't fix it, by golly, I'll fix it myself.
"Golly gee, mister, thanks!" the kid said, sounding like a 1950s TV show.
He counted the change twice and said, "By golly, she was right."
entries.русский: ей-богу! — устар. смягчённое by God; само golly — простодушное «ух ты»
entries.variants: golly, golly gee, gollee, by golly gee, golly gee whiz

entries.meaning: Another swap for by God, this one associated with old farmers, Yorkshire transplants, and Midwestern stubbornness. It punctuates a determined statement or a satisfying discovery.
examples: "By gum, I think you've got it."
We'll finish this fence today, by gum.
By gum, if that isn't the same car he drove in high school.
She tightened the last bolt. "By gum, that ought to hold."
"By gum, they don't make them like that anymore."
entries.русский: ей-богу!, чёрт побери — устар. замена by God, речь старых фермеров
entries.variants: by gum it, I'll be gum-swizzled

entries.meaning: A Victorian-era oath of emphasis, famous enough that a bellicose 1870s song gave English the word jingoism. As an interjection it now sounds thoroughly antique and is used with a grin.
examples: "By jingo, we'll be there by nightfall."
By jingo, that's the fastest I've ever seen him move.
He read the telegram twice. "By jingo, they've done it."
We're going to win this thing, by jingo, or die trying.
"By the living jingo, you've outdone yourself, Mrs. Petrie."
entries.русский: ей-ей!, чёрт возьми — устар. викторианская божба (отсюда «джингоизм»)
entries.variants: by jingoes, by the living jingo

entries.meaning: A wide-eyed exclamation of surprise or mild complaint, and originally a way to start saying Jesus and stop in time. It reads as boyish and innocent, which is why gee-whiz has also become an adjective for anything flashily impressive.
examples: "Gee whiz, do we have to do this again?"
Gee whiz, that's a beautiful piece of work.
The presentation was all gee-whiz graphics and no actual numbers.
"Gee whiz, Mom, I was just asking."
Gee whiz — I had no idea it cost that much.
entries.русский: ух ты!, ну надо же — устар. простодушное удивление, обрубленное Jesus
entries.variants: geez whiz, gee whizz, gee

entries.meaning: An elaborated gee whiz from the mid-1800s, now pure cartoon boy-detective. It expresses amazement, and any American over ten who says it is doing a bit.
examples: "Gee willikers, that thing can really fly!"
Gee willikers, look at all these presents.
He whistled at the scoreboard. "Gee whillikers."
Gee willikers, Batman, how did you figure it out?
"Gee willikers," she deadpanned, "what an absolutely thrilling meeting."
entries.русский: вот это да!, ух ты! — устар. развёрнутое gee whiz, речь мальчишек из комиксов
entries.variants: gee whillikers, gee willikins, golly willikers, gee willikers wow

entries.meaning: A clean substitute for good God, built on the same good + harmless noun pattern as good grief and good night. It expresses exasperated disbelief at something excessive.
examples: "Good gravy, how much did you buy?"
Good gravy, it's freezing in here.
He looked at the line out the door. "Good gravy, we'll be here all night."
Good gravy alive, would you two stop arguing?
"Good gravy, that's the fourth email he's sent this morning."
entries.русский: боже ты мой!, ну и ну — разг. приличная замена good God, досадливое недоверие
entries.variants: good gravy alive, great gravy, good gravy Marie
entries.see also: good grief, good night nurse, lordy

entries.meaning: A mild, weary expression of dismay, dodging good God the same way good gravy does. Charlie Brown made it a national catchphrase, so it carries a faint comic-strip sigh no matter who says it.
examples: "Good grief, not another meeting."
Good grief, look at this traffic.
She opened the bill and said, "Oh good grief."
Good grief, you two, it was a joke.
"Good grief," he sighed, picking the toys up off the floor again.
entries.русский: боже мой!, вот наказание — разг. усталая досада (реплика Чарли Брауна)
entries.variants: oh good grief, good grief Charlie Brown
entries.see also: good gravy, good night nurse, good grief

entries.meaning: A 1920s exclamation of astonishment or dismay meaning roughly that's the end of that or would you look at this. It is very dated and now shows up mainly in the Mountain West, in Utah, and from people who learned it from a grandparent.
examples: "Good night nurse, how did the kitchen get like this?"
Good night, that's a steep hill.
He fumbled the pass at the goal line. "Good night nurse."
Good night nurse, they've raised the rent again.
"Good night alive, you nearly gave me a heart attack."
entries.русский: вот это номер!, ну всё — устар. изумление или досада, слэнг 1920-х
entries.variants: good night, good night alive, good grief nurse
entries.see also: good grief, good gravy, great Scott

entries.meaning: A florid oath of astonishment, permanently attached to Perry White, the shouting newspaper editor of the Superman stories. Anyone using it now is being deliberately grandiose.
examples: "Great Caesar's ghost, who let this go to print?"
Great Caesar's ghost, that's a lot of money for a sandwich.
He threw open the door. "Great Caesar's ghost, what happened in here?"
Great Caesar, man, you scared the daylights out of me.
"Great Caesar's ghost," the coach yelled, "block somebody!"
entries.русский: святые угодники! — устар. напыщенное изумление (возглас Перри Уайта)
entries.variants: great Caesar, great Caesar's ghost alive

entries.meaning: A nineteenth-century American oath of alarm or astonishment, probably softened from great God and possibly nodding at General Winfield Scott. It got a second life from Doc Brown in Back to the Future, so younger Americans hear it as a mad-scientist word.
examples: "Great Scott, we're going to be late!"
Great Scott, look at the size of that hailstone.
He checked the meter and said, "Great Scott, the power's still on."
Great Scott, man, you can't just walk in there.
"Great Scott!" she said, in her best Doc Brown voice. "The car's out of gas."
entries.русский: боже правый!, вот те раз — устар. возглас тревоги или изумления
entries.variants: great Scott alive, great Scot
entries.see also: great Caesar's ghost, good night nurse, egad

entries.meaning: An exclamation of surprise or shock whose Betsy nobody has ever been able to identify. It sounds like a maiden aunt and is used today with affection, irony, or both; the Hanna-Barbera variant heavens to Murgatroyd is even more of a joke.
examples: "Heavens to Betsy, look what the wind did to the porch."
Heavens to Betsy, child, where are your shoes?
She read the headline and said, "Well, heavens to Betsy."
Heavens to Murgatroyd, they've changed the recipe.
"Heavens to Betsy, I nearly walked right past you."
entries.русский: батюшки светы! — устар. удивление; звучит как речь старой тётушки
entries.variants: heavens to Murgatroyd, heavens above, heavens
entries.see also: my stars, land sakes, heavens to Betsy

entries.meaning: An old-fashioned yelp of delight, dating to the 1890s and peaking with the crooners of the 1940s. It celebrates good news you have just heard, and the fuller hot diggity dog is even bouncier.
examples: "Hot dog! Payday came early."
Hot diggity dog, we got the house.
He opened the box, saw the fishing reel, and said, "Hot dog."
Hot diggity, look at that spread — is that all homemade?
"Hot dog," Grandpa said, "the Cubs actually won one."
entries.русский: ура!, вот здорово! — устар. радостный вопль по поводу хорошей новости
entries.variants: hot diggity dog, hot diggity, hot ziggity, hot dog almighty

entries.meaning: A soft-pedaled Jesus, expressing surprise, worry, or gentle protest. Jeepers creepers is the sing-song extension, borrowed from the 1938 song and now with a horror-movie shadow on it.
examples: "Jeepers, you scared me."
Jeepers creepers, where'd you get those peepers?
Jeepers, that's a long drive for one meeting.
"Jeepers, Dad, I said I was sorry."
She looked over the cliff edge and said, "Jeepers, that's high."
entries.русский: ой-ой-ой!, батюшки — устар. смягчённое Jesus: испуг, тревога, лёгкий упрёк
entries.variants: jeepers creepers, jeeps, jeez

entries.meaning: A minced Jesus Christ that has been in American mouths since the 1800s and got a friendly face from Disney's Pinocchio in 1940. It marks startled surprise or exasperation and is completely safe in front of children.
examples: "Jiminy cricket, that door is loud."
Jiminy Christmas, how many boxes did you order?
He hit his head on the cabinet. "Jiminy crickets!"
Jiminy cricket, it's already dark out.
"Jiminy, would you look at that sunset."
entries.русский: ёлки-палки!, батюшки — устар. смягчённое Jesus Christ, вполне детское
entries.variants: jiminy crickets, jiminy Christmas, jiminy, jimmity Christmas

entries.meaning: A wonderfully overblown oath naming a king of Judah instead of the Lord. It expresses astonishment, usually at something sudden or enormous, and it is now performed rather than merely said.
examples: "Jumpin' Jehoshaphat, that thing came out of nowhere!"
Jumping Jehoshaphat, look at the price of beef.
He opened the water bill. "Great Jehoshaphat."
Jumpin' Jehoshaphat, you two are loud this morning.
"Jumpin' Jehoshaphat," the sheriff said, "who taught you to drive?"
entries.русский: святые угодники!, мать честная — устар. нарочито пышное изумление
entries.variants: jumping Jehoshaphat, great Jehoshaphat, by Jehoshaphat
entries.see also: great Caesar's ghost, great Scott, what in Sam Hill

entries.meaning: Sam Hill is a nineteenth-century stand-in for hell, so the phrase is a clean way to demand what the hell is going on. Like tarnation, it lives almost entirely inside questions.
examples: "What in Sam Hill do you think you're doing?"
Where in Sam Hill did that dog get to?
What the Sam Hill is that noise coming from the basement?
"Who in Sam Hill signed off on this?" the foreman asked.
How in Sam Hill am I supposed to get there by six?
entries.русский: какого чёрта — устар. Sam Hill = приличная замена hell, только в вопросах
entries.variants: Sam Hill, who in Sam Hill, where in Sam Hill, what the Sam Hill

entries.meaning: A Middle English cry of sorrow, dead in ordinary speech for centuries and alive today only as costume. Americans use it in the fixed pair alas and alack to make a mock-tragic show of a small misfortune.
examples: "Alas and alack, the coffee machine is broken again."
Alack, the last slice of pizza is gone.
He clapped a hand to his forehead. "Alack the day!"
Alas and alack — no tickets left for the early show.
"Alack," she said, entirely without sincerity, "the meeting has been canceled."
entries.русский: увы!, о горе! — устар. книжн. скорбь; сегодня лишь шутливо (alas and alack)
entries.variants: alack the day, alas and alack, alack-a-day

entries.meaning: A seventeenth-century softening of ah God, now the standard interjection for anyone imitating a fussy Victorian gentleman. It marks surprise, dismay, or theatrical alarm.
examples: "Egad, man, put some clothes on!"
Egad, this coffee is strong.
He opened the ledger and muttered, "Egad, we're in trouble."
Egads, is that the time?
"Egad," said the professor, peering into the microscope, "it's moving."
entries.русский: ей-богу!, вот те на — устар. смягчённое ah God, речь чопорного викторианца
entries.variants: egads, 'egad, ye gods

entries.meaning: A medieval expression of disgust or reproach — the Elizabethan shame on you. It is entirely archaic in America and surfaces only in Shakespeare, in fantasy games, and in jokes.
examples: "Fie on you and your terrible puns."
Fie! I'll not stand for such treachery.
He pushed the plate away. "Fie, this soup is cold."
Fie upon it — the wifi is out again.
"Fie, sir," she said, mock-offended, "you've taken my parking spot."
entries.русский: фу!, стыд и срам! — устар. средневековое отвращение или упрёк
entries.variants: fie on you, fie upon it, fie fie

entries.meaning: An archaic indeed or truly, used to affirm something. No modern American says it sincerely; it functions as a signal that the speaker is putting on a Renaissance-fair voice.
examples: "Forsooth, the printer hath jammed once more."
Is the meeting canceled? Forsooth, it is.
Forsooth, good sir, thy parking is atrocious.
He raised his plastic goblet. "Forsooth, this mead is decent."
"Forsooth," she typed in the group chat, "the deploy hath failed."
entries.русский: поистине, воистину — устар. книжн. подтверждение; сейчас только в стилизации
entries.variants: forsooth, good sir, in sooth

entries.meaning: Another chopped-up oath on God — probably God's hooks, meaning the nails of the crucifixion — from the same seventeenth-century family as zounds. It expresses startled amazement and is used now only in jest.
examples: "Gadzooks! Where did all these emails come from?"
Gadzooks, that dog is enormous.
He lifted the tarp off the engine. "Gadzooks, what a mess."
Gadzooks — I've locked myself out again.
"Gadzooks, milady," he said, holding the door with a flourish.
entries.русский: батюшки!, чёрт побери — устар. божба XVII в. (God's hooks), теперь лишь в шутку
entries.variants: gadzooks alive, odzooks

entries.meaning: An old command meaning listen — the word that opens the Christmas carol and every mock-medieval announcement. Modern Americans use it to make a joke of an entrance or an interruption.
examples: "Hark! I hear the ice cream truck."
Hark, the sound of the boss's footsteps.
He held up a hand. "Hark — is that thunder?"
Hark ye, citizens: the elevator is fixed.
"Hark," she announced from the doorway, "I have brought doughnuts."
entries.русский: чу!, слушай! — устар. книжн. призыв прислушаться
entries.variants: hark ye, hark now, hearken

entries.meaning: A contraction of I pray thee, meaning please, worn to a nub by the 1600s and gone from real American speech since. Today it appears only in period writing and in playful mock-formality, often alongside pray tell.
examples: "Prithee, good sir, pass the salt."
Prithee, tell me you saved the file.
He bowed slightly. "Prithee, after you."
Pray tell, how did you talk your way out of that one?
"I prithee, no more of your dad jokes tonight."
entries.русский: прошу тебя, будь любезен — устар. стяжённое I pray thee, то есть «пожалуйста»
entries.variants: pray thee, pray tell, I prithee

entries.meaning: A crushed form of God's wounds, once shocking enough to count as real blasphemy and now the most quaintly harmless word in English. The spelling pronunciation ZOWNDZ is what Americans use; the older ZOONDZ survives only among Shakespeareans.
examples: "Zounds! That is a large spider."
Zounds, the rent is due again already.
He drew his foam sword. "Zounds, villain, have at thee!"
Zounds — I completely forgot about the dentist.
"Zounds," he said, reading the group chat, "you people never sleep."
entries.русский: чёрт побери!, о ужас! — устар. от God's wounds: былое богохульство, ныне безобидно
entries.variants: 'zounds, zoonds

entries.meaning: The sailor's hail, shouted across water to get another vessel's attention. On land it is pure play — a jokey hello, sometimes with a nod to Alexander Graham Bell, who wanted ahoy-hoy to be the standard telephone greeting.
examples: "Ahoy there! Can you throw us a line?"
Ship ahoy — two points off the starboard bow.
He stuck his head into the kitchen. "Ahoy, anybody making coffee?"
Ahoy-hoy, this is Dave, leave a message.
"Land ho!" the lookout called, and everyone crowded to the rail.
entries.русский: эй, на судне!, эге-гей — мор. оклик через воду; на суше — шутливое приветствие
entries.variants: ahoy there, ship ahoy, land ho, ahoy-hoy

entries.meaning: The all-purpose pirate noise, a growled agreement, threat, or general seafaring punctuation. It is not historical sailor speech at all — it comes from Robert Newton's West Country accent in the 1950 film Treasure Island — and Americans use it only in costume, especially on Talk Like a Pirate Day.
examples: "Arr, there be treasure in that spreadsheet."
Yarr, ye scurvy dogs, back to work.
He put on the eye patch and growled, "Arrr."
Arr — I'll take the last slice, matey.
"Did you finish the report?" "Arr, captain."
entries.русский: арр — рычание киношного пирата: согласие, угроза или просто присказка
entries.variants: arrr, yarr, yarrr, arrgh

entries.meaning: A genuine old sea command meaning stop or hold fast, from Dutch houd vast. Ashore it lives only in pirate imitation, where it usually opens a mock-order.
examples: "Avast, ye landlubbers! Nobody touches the cake."
Avast — belay that line before it runs out.
He held up a spatula. "Avast there, that's my grill."
Avast, me hearties, the movie's starting.
"Avast ye," the tour guide said, entirely in character.
entries.русский: стой!, полундра — мор. устар. команда остановиться; ныне «пиратская» пародия
entries.variants: avast there, avast ye, avast, me hearties

entries.meaning: The driver's command telling a horse, mule, or sled dog team to turn right. It pairs with haw for left, and the two survive in the country saying that someone doesn't know gee from haw — meaning they know nothing at all. This is a separate word from the mild exclamation gee, which is a shortened Jesus.
examples: "Gee!" the teamster called, and the mules swung right.
Gee — take the fork by the creek.
He whistled once and shouted gee, and the lead dog turned.
Old Bess knows gee and haw better than most drivers know their turn signals.
"That boy doesn't know gee from haw," Grandpa said, not unkindly.
entries.русский: но, направо! — команда лошади или упряжке повернуть вправо (пара к haw)
entries.variants: gee up, gee haw, gee over

entries.meaning: Get up, worn smooth, said to a horse to make it start moving. Off the trail it has become a cheerful let's get going, sometimes with a slap on the table or a hand-slap on an imaginary flank.
examples: "Giddyup!" she said, and the pony started down the path.
All right, team — coats on, shoes on, giddyup.
He finished his coffee, stood, and said, "Giddyup, we're burning daylight."
Giddyap, boy, we've got ten miles to cover before dark.
The kid bounced on the couch cushion yelling giddyup at nobody in particular.
entries.русский: но!, пошёл! — понукание лошади; в переносном смысле «поехали, шевелись»
entries.variants: giddy-up, giddyap, git up, hyah, giddyup now

entries.meaning: The command for a left turn, the partner of gee. It belongs to plow horses, ox teams, and dogsleds, and outside farming and mushing communities most Americans know it only from the phrase gee and haw.
examples: "Haw!" he called, and the team leaned into the turn.
Haw — bring them around toward the barn.
The musher shouted haw and the sled swung left onto the river trail.
My grandfather could plow a straight row on nothing but gee and haw.
"Haw, now, easy," she said, steadying the plow handles.
entries.русский: налево! — команда лошади или упряжке повернуть влево (пара к gee)
entries.variants: haw now, gee haw, haw over

entries.meaning: The sing-song call used to bring hogs to the trough, built on the same pattern as here kitty kitty. Americans mostly use it jokingly now — at a buffet, at a slow-moving friend, or at their own dog.
examples: "Here piggy piggy!" the farmer called, banging the feed bucket.
Here piggy, come on, breakfast.
He waved a doughnut at his brother. "Here piggy piggy."
Here pig pig — she's got apples for you.
"Here piggy piggy," my uncle sang as he carried the slop bucket to the pen.
entries.русский: чух-чух-чух! — подзывание свиней к кормушке; сейчас чаще в шутку
entries.variants: here piggy piggy, here pig pig, sooey pig

entries.meaning: The storybook command to start a dog team, probably worn down from French Canadian marche. Real Alaskan mushers usually shout hike or all right instead, so mush is best understood as the popular, literary version — and as a joke Americans make when they want someone to hurry.
examples: "Mush!" he shouted, and the team leaned into the traces.
Mush on, boys, we've got twenty miles to the checkpoint.
She grabbed the sled rope and yelled mush at her laughing kids.
Mush, you huskies — it's a line from every dogsled movie ever made.
"Come on, mush," he told the dog, who did not move.
entries.русский: вперёд! — команда собачьей упряжке трогаться (книжно-киношная)
entries.variants: mush on, mush, you huskies, hike

entries.meaning: The traditional hog call, hollered across a field to bring the pigs in. Its most famous outing is the Arkansas Razorback cheer Woo Pig Sooie, which is why the word now means football to as many Americans as it means livestock.
examples: "Sooey! Come on now, sooey!"
He cupped his hands and let out a sooey you could hear two farms over.
Woo pig sooie — the whole stadium calls it together.
Grandma could call the hogs with one soo-ey and a bucket.
"Pig sooey," the kid yelled, mostly to see how loud he could be.
entries.русский: чух-чух!, свиньи, сюда! — традиционный клич, сзывающий свиней (кричалка Арканзаса)
entries.variants: soo-ey, soo-ee, pig sooey, woo pig sooie

entries.meaning: The command to stop a horse, and by extension the word Americans use to slow anybody down — a driver, a talker, or a plan getting ahead of itself. The horse sense is the folksy one; the same syllable also works as plain surprise, which is a separate use covered elsewhere. Note the spelling: whoa is standard and woah is a common misspelling.
examples: "Whoa, girl," he said, easing back on the reins.
Whoa there — nobody said anything about spending money.
Whoa Nelly, that's a lot of paperwork for one permit.
He put a hand out. "Whoa, back up. Who told you that?"
"Whoa now," the farrier murmured, running a hand down the horse's leg.
entries.русский: тпру! — команда лошади остановиться; в переносном смысле «стоп, притормози»
entries.variants: whoa there, whoa now, whoa Nelly, woah

entries.meaning: The cowboy whoop of exhilaration, let out at rodeos, on dance floors, and any time a pickup truck goes over a hill too fast. Outside the West it is often used with a knowing grin, and yee-haw has become shorthand for country culture generally.
examples: "Yee-haw!" he hollered as the truck bounced through the field.
Yee-haw, school's out for the summer.
The band started up and half the room answered with a yee-haw.
She got the promotion and texted back a single yeehaw.
"Yee-hah!" the kid yelled, hanging onto the pony for dear life.
entries.русский: и-ха!, ух-ты-ы! — ковбойский вопль восторга
entries.variants: yeehaw, yee-hah, yee-hoo, ya-hoo

entries.meaning: A 1920s verdict meaning the very best, from a fad for nonsense superlatives built out of animal parts. It is used as a one-phrase exclamation of approval, always with the, and always with a whiff of flapper costume.
examples: "That new bakery? The bee's knees."
She thinks her grandson is the bee's knees.
The bee's knees — that's what my grandmother called anything she loved.
He tried the coffee, closed his eyes, and said, "Bee's knees."
Two dollars for a haircut and a shave? The bee's knees.
entries.русский: высший класс, лучше некуда — устар. слэнг 1920-х, всегда с the
entries.variants: the bee's knees, the bees knees

entries.meaning: The twin of the bee's knees, from the same 1920s craze, meaning something outstanding. The cat's meow is the equally common variant, and both are now used with deliberate old-timey charm.
examples: "This milkshake is the cat's pajamas."
He thought that car was the cat's meow.
The cat's pajamas — I've never heard anyone under seventy say it seriously.
"Oh, she's the cat's whiskers, that one," Grandpa said fondly.
New porch, new grill, new chairs — the cat's pajamas.
entries.русский: высший класс, то что надо — устар. слэнг 1920-х, близнец bee's knees
entries.variants: the cat's pajamas, the cat's meow, the cat's whiskers, cat's pyjamas

entries.meaning: A goofy, harmless that's great, popular from the late 1970s through the 1990s and now a mild dad-joke of a phrase. It answers good but low-stakes news.
examples: "I got us a table at seven." "Cool beans."
Cool beans, I'll see you there.
She shrugged. "Free parking? Cool beans."
"Cool beans," he said, and everyone groaned at how dated he sounded.
The download finished early — cool beans.
entries.русский: круто!, здорово! — разг. добродушное одобрение, слэнг 1980–90-х
entries.variants: cool beans, man, coolbeans

entries.meaning: Counterculture approval from the late 1960s, meaning wonderfully strange or just wonderful. It is drawn out when spoken, and using it today marks you as either very old or very ironic.
examples: "They're playing the whole album live?" "Far out."
Far out, man, I had no idea you played bass.
He looked at the mural for a long moment. "Faaar out."
Far out — she biked across the entire state.
The whole festival was a far-out scene, top to bottom.
entries.русский: офигеть!, потрясающе — устар. хипповское одобрение конца 1960-х
entries.variants: faaar out, way out, far-out

entries.meaning: The definitive 1960s word for excellent, from jazz musicians playing in the groove. Nobody says it straight anymore; it now signals either nostalgia or a joke about hippies.
examples: "Dinner at seven?" "Groovy."
Groovy, I'll bring the record player.
She'd painted the whole van orange. "Groovy," he said, meaning it.
Groovy — we've got the place to ourselves all weekend.
"That is one groovy shirt, Dad."
entries.русский: клёво, классно — устар. главное слово 1960-х; сегодня только с иронией
entries.variants: groovy baby, real groovy

entries.meaning: A World War II-era noise of open admiration, originally hollered by soldiers at a passing woman. It is now used almost entirely as a joke — often about food or a nice suit — because the leering original is genuinely unwelcome; do not aim it at a stranger.
examples: "Hubba hubba, look at that pie."
He came downstairs in the tuxedo and his wife said, "Hubba hubba."
Hubba hubba — somebody bought a new truck.
She modeled the dress for her friends, who all went hubba hubba.
"Hubba hubba," the old sailor said, and immediately apologized for it.
entries.русский: ух ты, хороша! — устар. одобрительный присвист; сейчас лишь в шутку
entries.variants: hubba-hubba, hubba

entries.meaning: A 1950s and 60s children's word for cool, still spoken by adults who want to sound cheerfully square. The rhyming extension neato burrito is playground-grade silly.
examples: "Neato, a whole box of comics."
Neato burrito, they've got waffle fries.
He watched the drone lift off. "Neato."
Neato — I didn't know the library did that.
"Look, the fish are blue." "Neat-o."
entries.русский: клёво, здорово — устар. детское словечко 1950–60-х вместо cool
entries.variants: neat-o, neato burrito, neat-o keen, neat

entries.meaning: Late-1960s and 70s praise meaning so good it is beyond looking at. It belongs to the same soul-and-hippie vocabulary as far out and right on, and it is said with a rising, delighted tone.
examples: "The band was outta sight."
Out of sight — you got front-row seats?
He tasted the sauce and said, "Outta sight, man."
Outta sight, they're paying for the whole trip.
"Your new place is out of sight," she said, spinning around the living room.
entries.русский: улёт!, обалдеть! — устар. похвала конца 1960-х и 70-х
entries.variants: out of sight, outasight

entries.meaning: A 1950s way of saying wonderful, wholesome enough for a soda fountain. Watch the tone: just peachy is almost always sarcastic in modern American speech, meaning things are going badly.
examples: "How was the interview?" "Peachy keen."
Keen! A new bike for my birthday!
Everything's just peachy — the car won't start and it's raining.
She said the arrangement was peachy keen with her.
"Peachy keen, jelly bean," my aunt says whenever anything works out.
entries.русский: чудесно, лучше не бывает — устар. слэнг 1950-х; just peachy обычно саркастично
entries.variants: peachy, keen, just peachy, peachy keen jelly bean

entries.meaning: Emphatic agreement and solidarity, out of Black American speech and into the counterculture of the late 1960s. It says yes, exactly, I'm with you, and it often comes with a raised fist or a nod.
examples: "We're not paying for parking twice." "Right on."
Right on, man, that's what I've been saying all along.
He heard the plan and just said, "Right on."
Right on — glad somebody finally said it out loud.
"You quit? Right on," she said, high-fiving him.
entries.русский: вот именно!, точно! — разг. решительное согласие и поддержка
entries.variants: right on, man, right on right on
entries.see also: far out, outta sight, right on

entries.meaning: The all-American word for great from roughly 1900 to 1955, still instantly readable and still faintly black-and-white. Modern speakers use it either fondly or, very often, sarcastically: oh, that's just swell means the opposite of swell.
examples: "Swell! I'll pick you up at six."
That's a swell idea — let's do it.
Flat tire in the rain. "Oh, swell."
He's a swell guy once you get to know him.
"How's the new job?" "Just swell," she said flatly, and changed the subject.
entries.русский: отлично, здорово — устар. слэнг 1900–1955; сегодня часто саркастично
entries.variants: just swell, swell guy, oh swell

entries.meaning: A 1920s catchphrase meaning let's get out of here or scram, often told as a story about wind and short skirts at the Flatiron Building. It is now the single most museum-piece phrase in American slang, understood by everyone and used sincerely by no one.
examples: "Cops are coming — twenty-three skidoo!"
23 skidoo, we're not sticking around for the speeches.
He grabbed his hat. "Skidoo, boys."
Twenty-three skidoo — that's my entire impression of the 1920s.
"Skiddoo," the bartender said, jerking a thumb toward the door.
entries.русский: сматываемся!, тикаем отсюда — устар. слэнг 1920-х, чистый музейный экспонат
entries.variants: 23 skidoo, skidoo, skiddoo

entries.meaning: Northern California's homegrown intensifier, from hell of a, meaning very or a lot of. It works mostly in front of another word (hella good, hella people), but Bay Area speakers also fire it off alone as a one-word absolutely. The clean version hecka is what kids say in front of teachers.
examples: "Was the line long?" "Hella."
That burrito was hella good.
There were hella people at the beach on Saturday.
Hella — I've been saying that since middle school and I'm not stopping.
"It's hecka cold in here," she said, borrowing his jacket.
entries.русский: очень, куча — диал. (Сев. Калифорния) усилитель от hell of a; отдельно — «ещё как»
entries.variants: hecka, hella good, hells of

entries.meaning: Did you eat?, run together until it is a single syllable — a conversational opener in Pittsburgh, Philadelphia, and across the South and Midwest. The traditional reply compresses the same way: no, joo? for did you? Write it out only when you are transcribing dialect on purpose.
examples: "Jeet yet?" "Naw, joo?"
He walked in the door and the first thing his mother said was "Jeet?"
Jeet already, or should I put a plate together?
"Jeetjet?" is a whole Pittsburgh greeting in one syllable.
My grandfather's version of hello was "Jeet, hon?"
entries.русский: поел?, ты ел? — диал. слитное did you eat? (Питтсбург, Филадельфия, Юг, Средний Запад)
entries.variants: jeet yet, jeetjet, djeet

entries.meaning: A clipped, swallowed oh that Midwesterners emit on any small collision with the world — bumping a cart, dropping a fork, or needing to get past someone. It is an apology, a startle, and a social lubricant all at once, and it is the single most reliable Midwestern tell.
examples: "Ope, sorry, didn't see you there."
Ope — let me just sneak right past ya.
He knocked the pen off the counter. "Ope."
Ope, that's my phone ringing.
"Ope, I think I took your coffee," she said, swapping the cups back.
entries.русский: ой!, упс — диал. (Средний Запад) короткое «ой» при мелкой оплошности
entries.variants: ope, sorry, ope, lemme just squeeze past ya

entries.meaning: A Norwegian import that settled in Minnesota, the Dakotas, and Wisconsin, covering everything a sigh covers: fatigue, sympathy, mild disgust, and being overwhelmed. The first vowel is the short one in book, not the one in cuff. It is the Upper Midwest's all-purpose release valve, printed on more bumper stickers than any other word in the region.
examples: "Uff da, that was a long drive."
Forty below with the wind chill? Uff da.
She lifted the casserole dish out of the oven. "Uff da, that's heavy."
Uff da — I ate way too much lefse.
"He backed into the mailbox again?" "Oofta."
entries.русский: ух!, ой-ой-ой — диал. (Миннесота, Дакоты) из норвежского: усталость, сочувствие, «сил нет»
entries.variants: uffda, uff-da, oofta, oofda

entries.meaning: New England's intensifier, meaning very — wicked good, wicked cold, wicked far. Boston and Maine speakers also use it alone as a shout of approval, roughly awesome. Note that in the intensifier use it does not mean evil at all, and it stays an adverb: wicked good, never wicked well.
examples: "They won in overtime." "Wicked."
That chowder is wicked good.
It's wicked cold out on the water this morning.
Wicked — my cousin got us into the game for free.
"The new bridge is wicked pissah," he said, which is about as Boston as a sentence gets.
entries.русский: очень, жутко — диал. (Новая Англия) усилитель: wicked good = «жутко хорошо»
entries.variants: wicked good, wicked pissah, wicked awesome

entries.meaning: Hearty Upper Midwestern agreement, meaning yes, absolutely and also serving as a cheerful you're welcome. Fargo and a generation of Minnesota politicians have made it the region's signature phrase, so outside the Midwest it often comes with an accent attached.
examples: "Can you have it done by Friday?" "You betcha."
Thanks for the ride. "Oh, you betcha, anytime."
Ya betcha we're going to the lake this weekend.
"Cold enough for ya?" "You betcha it is."
She answered every request with a you betcha and a smile.
entries.русский: а как же!, ещё бы! — диал. (Верхний Средний Запад) согласие; также «не за что»
entries.variants: ya betcha, you betcha by golly, oh you betcha

entries.meaning: Yiddish for nothing at all, literally goat droppings, used as a scornful one-word verdict on a payout, an effort, or a result. It carries a shrug and a sneer, and it is understood far beyond New York.
examples: "What did you get out of the settlement?" "Bubkes."
We searched all afternoon and found bupkis.
He worked there twelve years and they gave him bubkes.
Bupkis — that's what her research turned up.
"Any news?" "Bubkes. Not a word."
entries.русский: шиш, ни шиша — разг. из идиша: «совсем ничего» (букв. козий помёт)
entries.variants: bupkis, bupkes, bubkis, bopkes

entries.meaning: A short Yiddish puff of contempt, aimed at something distasteful, cheap, or beneath comment. It is smaller and drier than ugh — a dismissal rather than a reaction.
examples: "Feh. I wouldn't eat that on a dare."
Reality television? Feh.
She looked at the price tag and said, "Feh, for this?"
Feh — he's been telling that same story for thirty years.
"How was the movie?" "Feh."
entries.русский: фу, тьфу — разг. из идиша: короткое сухое презрение, отмашка
entries.variants: feh!, fe

entries.meaning: A Yiddish prod meaning well?, so?, or and then what? Said with a rising tone, it asks someone to get on with the story or to justify themselves; said flat, it is a resigned so it goes.
examples: "Nu? What did the doctor say?"
Nu, are we ordering or are we just going to read the menu all night?
He stood in the doorway with his hands up. "Nu?"
So the car broke down, nu, these things happen.
"Nu, so tell me already — did she say yes?"
entries.русский: ну?, и что? — разг. из идиша: побуждение продолжать; ровным тоном — «ну и ладно»
entries.variants: nu?, nu nu, so nu

entries.meaning: The basic Yiddish groan, carried into general American English through New York. It handles weariness, mild pain, worry, and comic despair, and stretching it out (oy yoy yoy) stretches the feeling to match.
examples: "Oy, my back."
Oy, three more forms to fill out.
She looked at the pile of dishes and said, "Oy oy oy."
Oy — don't remind me about the tax deadline.
"Oy yoy yoy, what a day," he said, dropping into the chair.
entries.русский: ой — разг. из идиша: усталость, лёгкая боль, тревога, комическое отчаяние
entries.variants: oy oy oy, oy yoy yoy, oy, oy

entries.meaning: The alarmed cousin of oy vey: gevalt is Yiddish for force or violence, and the phrase amounts to a cry for help. It marks genuine shock or a disaster in progress, not just weariness.
examples: "Oy gevalt, the basement is flooding!"
Gevalt — he told them what?
She saw the dented fender and said, "Oy gevalt, my father is going to kill me."
Oy gevalt, they've canceled the flight and the next one's tomorrow.
"Oy gevalt," the rabbi said, "who scheduled two weddings on the same afternoon?"
entries.русский: ой, караул!, спасите — разг. из идиша: настоящий испуг, беда на глазах
entries.variants: gevalt, oy gevald, gevalt geshrign

entries.meaning: Oh, woe — the full form of the groan, used for troubles large and small. The extended oy vey iz mir (oh, woe is me) turns up the drama, usually with humor attached, and the whole family of phrases now belongs to American English generally, not only to Jewish speakers.
examples: "Oy vey, another meeting about the meeting."
Oy vey iz mir, the car won't start again.
He read the group chat and muttered, "Oy vey."
Oy vey — she invited all four of her ex-husbands to the party.
"Traffic on the bridge, construction on the tunnel. Oy vey."
entries.русский: ой-вэй!, о горе мне — разг. из идиша: стон о бедах больших и малых
entries.variants: oy vey iz mir, oi vey, oy veh, oy vay
